title: Vision and Mission
questions: What is the company trying to achieve?
text:
The company's vision is to make information instantly accessible through natural conversation. The underlying belief is that most organisational knowledge already exists somewhere — in documents, wikis, product pages, policies, ticket histories, and the heads of colleagues — but that finding it costs far more time and effort than it should. Conventional search returns a list of links and leaves the reader to do the work of reading, filtering, and interpreting. The company's answer is a conversational interface that reads on the user's behalf, returns a direct answer grounded in the organisation's own material, and, where appropriate, carries out the follow-up action instead of merely describing it.

The mission that follows from this vision has two halves. The first is to reduce search effort: a person asking a question should get an answer, not a reading list. The second is to accelerate action: once the answer is known, the platform should be able to trigger the next step — send the notification, start the workflow, route the request — without forcing the user to switch to another system and start again. The company measures its own success by whether users stop needing to know where information lives and whether repetitive requests stop consuming human attention.

The vision deliberately excludes certain directions. The company is not building a general-purpose consumer assistant, a public web search engine, an open-domain knowledge product, or a model training company. It builds a platform that answers questions from a defined, customer-supplied body of knowledge and acts within a defined, customer-approved set of tools. Everything else in this corpus should be read as serving that narrower purpose.

title: The Business Problem the Company Solves
questions: What problem does the chatbot solve?
Why would a company need this chatbot?
text:
Organisations answer the same questions over and over again. Website visitors ask what a product does, whether it supports a particular use case, and how to get in touch. Employees ask what the travel policy says, where a template lives, who approves a request, and how a process works. Partners ask about integration details, commercial terms, and status. Stakeholders ask for figures and updates. Each individual question is easy; the aggregate is expensive. Support staff, subject-matter experts, and managers spend a substantial share of their working time retrieving information that already exists and relaying it to whoever asked.

This repetition creates several distinct costs. There is the direct labour cost of staff answering known questions. There is the delay cost, because a question asked outside business hours waits until someone is available. There is the inconsistency cost, because different people answer the same question differently and older answers circulate after the underlying policy has changed. There is the opportunity cost of interrupting specialists for routine lookups. And there is the abandonment cost on public websites, where a visitor who cannot quickly find an answer leaves rather than asking.

The chatbot addresses these costs by providing instant answers drawn from the organisation's own approved material, by locating information across sources the user would otherwise have to search individually, by routing requests to the correct team when a human genuinely is required, and by automating the workflows that commonly follow a question. The result is that repetitive support work decreases, response times fall to near zero for known questions, and the answers that people receive stay consistent with the source documents because they are generated from those documents each time rather than remembered by a person.

title: Product Summary
questions: What products does the company offer?
How is it different from a FAQ bot?
text:
The product is an agentic AI chatbot platform. It acts as a unified access point to an organisation's knowledge and processes, serving customers, employees, business partners, and stakeholders through a single conversational interface. It can be embedded in a public website or placed inside an internal portal, and the same deployment can serve both audiences with different knowledge and different permissions depending on who is asking.

The platform combines four technical building blocks. Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplies the chatbot with relevant passages from the organisation's own documents before an answer is written. Large Language Models turn those passages and the user's question into a fluent, direct answer. Tool calling allows the chatbot to invoke defined functions in external systems rather than only producing text. Workflow automation strings those calls together so that a multi-step business process can be completed inside the conversation.

The capabilities that result are question answering, website navigation, information retrieval, agentic task execution, email notification, and support for cross-team collaboration. Question answering covers factual questions about products, policies, and processes. Website navigation means the chatbot can point a user to, or move a user to, the correct page rather than describing where it is. Information retrieval covers finding a specific document, clause, figure, or record. Agentic task execution means completing a requested action, not merely explaining how to perform it. Email notification means the chatbot can send a message to the right recipient when a conversation warrants it. Cross-team collaboration means a request raised in one part of the organisation can be routed and tracked into another.

title: Who the Product Is For
text:
Four audiences use the chatbot, and the platform is designed to treat them differently. Customers and prospective customers interact with the public deployment on a company website. They ask about products, capabilities, pricing pages, availability, and how to make contact. They are anonymous by default, they see only public knowledge, and the actions available to them are limited to safe ones such as requesting contact or navigating the site.

Employees interact with an internal deployment inside a portal or intranet. They ask about internal policies, processes, tools, and records, and they can trigger workflows that affect internal systems. They are identified through the organisation's existing authentication, and what they can see and do follows the role assigned to them.

Business partners sit between the two. They are identified, they see a scoped subset of knowledge relevant to the partnership, and they may be permitted a limited set of actions such as status enquiries or ticket creation. Stakeholders, including management and other internal audiences with reporting needs, typically use the platform to retrieve consolidated information rather than to execute tasks.

The buyer within a customer organisation is usually a leader responsible for support, internal communications, IT, digital, or operations. The technical evaluator is usually IT or security. The day-to-day owner after deployment is usually whoever maintains the underlying knowledge — because in a retrieval-augmented system, maintaining the knowledge is maintaining the product.

title: System Architecture Overview
questions: What does the architecture look like?
How does a request flow through the system?
text:
The platform is composed of five logical layers. The ingestion layer takes in the customer's documents, website content, and internal knowledge, and prepares them for retrieval. The retrieval layer stores the prepared knowledge as vectors and finds the passages relevant to a given question. The reasoning layer is the Large Language Model together with the agent logic that plans, decides, and writes answers. The action layer is the set of tools and workflow integrations the agent may invoke. The governance layer runs across all of the others and covers authentication, permissions, knowledge scoping, logging, and compliance controls.

A single user request generally moves through these layers in order. The request arrives with an identity and a scope attached — anonymous public visitor, or an authenticated employee with a role. The governance layer resolves what knowledge and which tools that identity may reach. The retrieval layer searches only within the permitted knowledge scope. The reasoning layer plans an approach and either answers directly from the retrieved context or decides that one or more tools must be called. The action layer executes any approved tool calls. The reasoning layer then composes the final answer, and the governance layer records what happened.

The architecture separates knowledge from behaviour deliberately. Knowledge lives in the retrieval layer and is changed by updating documents. Behaviour lives in the agent configuration and tool definitions and is changed by configuration. This separation means that a customer can correct or extend what the chatbot knows without any engineering work, which is the main operational advantage of a retrieval-based design over a system where knowledge is embedded in code, prompts, or model weights.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Detail
questions: How does the chatbot avoid making things up?
text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation is the core technique behind the chatbot's factual answers. Rather than relying on what a language model absorbed during training, the system retrieves relevant passages from the customer's own document collection at the moment a question is asked and supplies those passages to the model as context. The model is then instructed to answer from that supplied context. The pipeline is: question, then embedding, then vector search, then retrieved context, then the Large Language Model, then the answer.

This design improves factual accuracy and reduces hallucinations for three reasons. First, the model is given the specific facts it needs at inference time, so it does not have to reconstruct them from imperfect memory. Second, the answer is anchored to text that actually exists in the organisation's documents, which makes it possible to show the user where an answer came from. Third, when retrieval returns nothing relevant, the system can detect that condition and have the model say it does not know, rather than allowing it to fill the gap with a plausible invention. A hallucination in a retrieval-grounded system is usually a retrieval failure or a prompting failure, and both are fixable without retraining anything.

The retrieval step matters more than any other single component. An answer can only be as good as the passages placed in front of the model, so the quality of chunking, embedding, and search determines the ceiling on answer quality. This is why the ingestion pipeline described in the next section receives disproportionate engineering attention relative to its apparent simplicity.

title: Ingestion, Chunking, and Embeddings
text:

Files are parsed according to type, converted to clean text, and stripped of navigation furniture, boilerplate, and markup that would pollute retrieval. The readable structure of the original — headings, sections, question-and-answer pairs, tables — is preserved as metadata because that structure carries meaning that flat text loses.

The cleaned text is then divided into chunks. A chunk is the unit that will be retrieved and shown to the model, so its size is a trade-off: chunks that are too small lose the context needed to interpret them, and chunks that are too large dilute the specific passage that answers the question and waste context window space. Chunking is therefore done along semantic boundaries wherever the source allows — by section, by heading, by paragraph group — rather than by cutting the text at a fixed character count. Adjacent chunks overlap slightly so that a sentence sitting on a boundary is not orphaned from the sentences that give it meaning. Each chunk is then converted into an embedding — a numerical vector, produced by an embedding model, that represents the meaning of the text as a position in a high-dimensional space. title: Query Processing and Retrieval
questions: How does it find the right document?
text:
When a user asks a question, the question is first prepared for search. Because conversations are continuous and questions are often elliptical — "and what about for contractors?" — the system resolves the question against the conversation history so that the text sent to the search engine is self-contained. The prepared question is then embedded using the same embedding model applied to the documents, producing a query vector in the same space.

The query vector is compared against the stored chunk vectors using a similarity measure, and the closest matches are returned. This is semantic search: it matches meaning rather than keywords, so it tolerates paraphrase, synonyms, and different phrasings of the same underlying question. Purely semantic search has a known weakness with exact identifiers — product codes, article numbers, specific names — where literal matching outperforms meaning matching. A hybrid approach that combines semantic similarity with keyword matching is therefore the standard mitigation, and results from both are merged before ranking.

Retrieval is always constrained by the access scope resolved for the requesting user. The filter is applied as part of the search itself rather than after it, so that content the user is not permitted to see is never retrieved, never reaches the model, and cannot leak through paraphrase. This is the single most important security property of the retrieval design.

title: Agentic AI and the Agent Loop
questions: How is it different from a FAQ bot?
Can the chatbot act on its own?
What stops the agent doing something wrong?
text:
The chatbot uses an agent architecture rather than a single question-in, answer-out exchange. An agent is a language model given a goal, a set of tools, and the ability to decide for itself which tools to use and in what order, observing the result of each step before choosing the next. It is capable of multi-step reasoning, tool selection, workflow execution, notification, and email automation, and it decomposes complex tasks into smaller actions before executing them.

In practice the agent runs a loop. It receives the user's request and the available context. It reasons about what the request actually requires and forms a plan. If the plan needs external information or an external effect, it selects a tool and produces the arguments for it. The platform executes that tool and returns the result. The agent observes the result, revises its plan if the result was unexpected, and either calls another tool or writes the final answer. The loop is bounded by a maximum number of steps so that a confused agent stops rather than looping indefinitely.

The difference from a FAQ bot is categorical rather than incremental. A FAQ bot maps a recognised question to a stored answer. An agent can answer a question that nobody anticipated by combining several retrieved facts, and it can change the state of the world — send the email, open the ticket, start the workflow — which a FAQ bot fundamentally cannot do. The difference from a plain RAG chatbot is narrower but still substantial: plain RAG retrieves once and answers, while an agent can retrieve, evaluate what it got, search again with a better query, and only then answer. Multi-step questions that require assembling several pieces of information are where this matters most.

title: Tool Calling and Workflow Automation
text:
Tool calling is the mechanism that lets a language model do something other than produce text. Each tool is defined by a name, a description of what it does and when it should be used, and a schema describing its parameters. Those definitions are supplied to the model, which, when it judges a tool appropriate, emits a structured request naming the tool and supplying arguments matching the schema. The platform — not the model — validates those arguments, checks the caller's permissions, executes the call against the target system, and returns the result to the model. The model never holds credentials and never talks to a target system directly; it only requests that the platform act on its behalf.

Workflow automation is the layer above individual tool calls. A workflow is a defined business process composed of several steps, potentially spanning several systems, with conditions and branches between them. A request that requires information to be looked up, a record to be created, a notification to be sent, and a confirmation to be returned is a workflow rather than a single action. The platform executes workflows in the same governed way it executes individual tools, with validation and permission checks at each step, logging throughout, and defined behaviour when a step fails: the failure is reported honestly to the user rather than being hidden behind an optimistic summary, and where a partial execution has occurred the user is told which steps completed.

title: Integrations
questions: What systems can it integrate with?
Does it connect to our intranet?
Can it post to Slack or Teams?
text:
The chatbot integrates with websites, internal knowledge bases, messaging systems, and email platforms in order to retrieve information and automate business processes. Website integration covers both the embedded chat interface itself and the ingestion of public site content as a knowledge source; it also enables navigation, where the chatbot takes the user to the relevant page rather than describing its location. Knowledge base integration covers document repositories, wikis, intranets, and file stores, and can be configured either as a periodic synchronisation into the vector index or as a live lookup at question time. Messaging integration allows the chatbot to post into team channels for notification and routing. Email integration allows outbound notification and confirmation.

Integrations fall into two functional categories that are worth distinguishing. Knowledge integrations bring information into the retrieval layer and are read-only by nature. Action integrations expose tools that let the agent do something in another system, and these carry write permissions that must be scoped tightly. A customer can enable knowledge integrations broadly with relatively low risk, whereas each action integration should be enabled deliberately, with the narrowest permission set that allows the intended task.

Technically, integrations are implemented against the target system's API using credentials supplied and owned by the customer. Credentials are stored encrypted, are never exposed to the language model, and are scoped to the minimum permissions the integration requires. Where a target system supports service accounts with restricted rights, a dedicated restricted account is preferred over a personal or administrative account. title: Knowledge Scopes and Access Control
questions: Can internal and public knowledge be separated?
text:
Separate knowledge scopes can be configured for public users and for employees. A knowledge scope is a labelled subset of the indexed corpus, and every chunk in the index carries the scope or scopes it belongs to. The public scope typically contains marketing material, product information, published documentation, and general company information. The internal scope typically contains policies, process documentation, internal records, and anything not intended for external readers. Further scopes can be defined for partners, for specific departments, or for particular roles.

Access control operates on the same principle as retrieval filtering described earlier: the scope is resolved from the requester's identity before the search runs, and the search is constrained to permitted scopes. Internal content is therefore not merely hidden from public users — it is never retrieved for them at all, which means it cannot appear in an answer, cannot be summarised, and cannot be extracted through indirect questioning. Content that is never placed in the model's context cannot be leaked by the model.

Permissions are configurable according to user roles, and the same principle extends from knowledge to actions: a role determines both what a user can be told and what the agent may do on that user's behalf. Public visitors are anonymous and receive the narrowest configuration. Authenticated users are identified through the customer's existing authentication system, so that the platform inherits the organisation's identity model rather than introducing a competing one. Role and scope configuration is owned by the customer, because only the customer can decide which of its own information belongs in which category.

A practical consequence worth stating plainly: correct scoping is a shared responsibility. The platform enforces the boundaries it is given, but it cannot know that a document placed in the public scope was meant to be confidential. Reviewing what goes into each scope is part of the customer's onboarding work and part of ongoing knowledge maintenance.

title: Delivery, Deployment, and Onboarding
questions: What do we need to provide?
text:
The delivery model is straightforward in outline. Customers provide company documents, website content, internal knowledge, and access policies. The company ingests that material, configures knowledge scopes, connects the agreed integrations, tunes the chatbot's behaviour and tone, and tests answer quality against a set of real questions before the deployment is opened to its intended audience.

Onboarding runs through several stages. In discovery, the customer's use cases, audiences, and the questions the chatbot is expected to handle are defined. In knowledge collection, the relevant material is gathered and, importantly, reviewed: material that is outdated, contradictory, or wrongly classified causes more retrieval problems than material that is merely sparse. In configuration, scopes, roles, integrations, and tools are set up. In tuning and testing, real questions are run against the system and answers are reviewed for accuracy, completeness, tone, and correct refusal behaviour on out-of-scope questions. In launch, the chatbot is embedded in the website or portal and made available to users. In operation, usage is monitored, gaps in knowledge are identified from real conversations, and the corpus is extended to close them.

The chatbot interface is embedded into an existing website or internal portal rather than replacing it, typically as a widget or an inline component, and it is styled to match the host environment. Because the platform is currently in its demonstration phase, deployment options, hosting arrangements, and service levels should be treated as subject to definition rather than as settled product facts; the current position on hosting region, tenancy model, and service level commitments is [PLACEHOLDER: hosting and service level details].

The single most important thing a customer can do to make a deployment succeed is to keep the source knowledge accurate and current. In a retrieval-based system, the documents are the product's memory. An outdated policy document produces confidently outdated answers, and no amount of model quality compensates for knowledge that is wrong at the source.

title: Security Practices
questions: How do you handle prompt injection?
How do I report a vulnerability?
text:
The platform is built around a set of standard security practices appropriate to a system that handles organisational knowledge. Data is encrypted in transit using current TLS, and data at rest — including the vector index, document store, and logs — is encrypted using industry-standard algorithms. Credentials for integrations and API keys are held in a secrets store, encrypted, rotated on a defined schedule, and never written into prompts, logs, or the model's context.

Access to production systems is restricted to authorised personnel, requires multi-factor authentication, and is granted on a least-privilege basis with periodic review. Administrative actions are logged. Application, access, and tool execution logs are retained for a defined period to support troubleshooting, security investigation, and audit, and log content is minimised so that sensitive material is not duplicated unnecessarily into logging systems.

Because the platform accepts untrusted input — anyone can type anything into a public chat window — specific attention is paid to the injection risks characteristic of language model systems. The design assumption is that model output may be influenced by adversarial input, so the security boundary is placed at the tool execution layer where it can be enforced deterministically.

text:
The platform follows GDPR principles, specifically transparency, lawful processing, purpose limitation, data minimisation, respect for user rights, and configurable access controls. This section states how those principles apply in practice and serves as the basis of the company's privacy policy for the chatbot product.

Roles and responsibilities. In a customer deployment, the customer organisation is normally the data controller for the personal data processed through its chatbot, because it decides what knowledge is loaded, which audiences are served, and what the chatbot is for. The company normally acts as data processor, processing personal data on the customer's documented instructions under a data processing agreement. For the company's own website and demonstration chatbot, the company is the controller. The template data processing agreement offered to customers is [PLACEHOLDER: link or reference to DPA].

Lawful basis. Processing is carried out on a lawful basis identified before processing begins. For business communication and service operation this is typically legitimate interest or the performance of a contract; where consent is the appropriate basis, such as for non-essential cookies or optional analytics, consent is collected before processing and can be withdrawn as easily as it was given. Purpose limitation means data collected to operate the chatbot is used to operate the chatbot and not repurposed for unrelated ends.

What is processed. A chatbot conversation may contain personal data, either because the user identifies themselves or because they mention personal details while asking a question. questions: Does the platform comply with the EU AI Act?
Will users know they are talking to an AI?
text:
The platform is designed to align with the evolving EU AI Act. Two obligations are directly relevant to a conversational system of this kind. The first is transparency: users must know they are interacting with an artificial intelligence system rather than a human. The chatbot therefore identifies itself as an AI assistant, does not claim to be a person, and does not adopt a persona that would mislead a user about its nature. The second is that additional obligations may apply where the system is deployed in a high-risk context — for example in employment, education, access to essential services, or other domains the Regulation classifies as high-risk. In such deployments, obligations relating to risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, human oversight, accuracy, and robustness may fall on the customer as deployer and on the company as provider, and these must be assessed before deployment rather than afterwards.

Because the Act's obligations are phased in over time and its interpretation continues to develop, the company's stated position is one of designing for alignment rather than asserting completed conformity. Concretely, this means maintaining documentation of how the system works, keeping logs sufficient to reconstruct what the system did and why, keeping a human in the loop for consequential actions, being explicit about limitations, and reassessing classification whenever a new deployment context is proposed. The company's current formal position on AI Act classification for its product is [PLACEHOLDER: AI Act risk classification assessment].

text:
Acceptable use. The platform is provided for legitimate business purposes. Customers agree not to use it to process categories of data outside the scope of the agreed deployment, to attempt to extract the underlying model or system prompts, to circumvent access controls, to send unsolicited bulk communication through the notification features, or to deploy it in a way that misleads users about the fact that they are interacting with an AI system. Human escalation. No automated system should be a dead end. Escalation is treated as a successful outcome, not a failure.

Content and conduct. The chatbot maintains a professional tone, does not produce discriminatory or harassing content, does not speculate about individuals, and does not disclose internal information to audiences outside the relevant knowledge scope. It does not make commercial commitments, quote prices, or agree contractual terms unless explicitly configured to do so with approved content.

title: Quality, Evaluation, and Monitoring
questions: How do you ensure answer quality?
What happens when it gets something wrong?
text:
Answer quality is treated as a measurable engineering property rather than an impression. Evaluation runs against a set of representative questions with known correct answers, and the properties assessed are retrieval quality — whether the correct passage was found at all — and answer quality — whether the response is faithful to the retrieved passages, complete, appropriately scoped, and correctly refuses when the knowledge base does not contain the answer. Separating these two measurements matters, because an incorrect answer caused by a retrieval miss is fixed in the ingestion pipeline while an incorrect answer drawn from correctly retrieved context is fixed in the prompt or the model configuration.

The most common failure modes and their standard remedies are worth recording. Retrieval misses are usually caused by poor chunking, a vocabulary mismatch between how users ask and how documents are written, or missing content, and are addressed by improving chunk boundaries, adding a hybrid keyword component, or extending the corpus. Answers that are technically supported but unhelpful are usually a context assembly problem, where the right passage was retrieved but buried among weaker ones. Confident answers about things not in the corpus indicate that the grounding instruction is too weak or the relevance threshold too permissive. Stale answers indicate a re-ingestion problem rather than a model problem.

In operation, monitoring covers conversation volume, resolution and escalation rates, latency, tool execution success and failure, and the questions that produced no confident answer. That last signal is the most valuable input to knowledge maintenance: a recurring unanswered question is a documented gap in the corpus, and closing it is a matter of writing the missing content. User feedback controls in the interface supply a direct quality signal alongside these metrics.

title: Limitations and Known Constraints
text:
Stating limitations plainly is part of the company's transparency commitment, and the chatbot should acknowledge them rather than deflect when asked.

The chatbot knows only what it is given. It has no knowledge of a customer's information beyond the material ingested into its index, and it cannot see systems it has not been integrated with. Its answers reflect the state of the source documents at the time of the most recent ingestion, so information that changed after that point will be answered from the older version until re-ingestion runs.

Language models can produce fluent text that is wrong. Retrieval grounding reduces this substantially but does not eliminate it, which is why answers are traceable to sources, why the system is instructed to admit ignorance, and why consequential actions require confirmation. For decisions with legal, financial, medical, or safety consequences, the output should be verified against the source document or with a qualified person.

The platform is currently a demonstration answering questions about its own product. It does not yet have deployed customer installations, and prospective customers should calibrate their expectations accordingly. Retrieval quality degrades where source material is contradictory, undated, duplicated across many near-identical versions, or written in a way that assumes context the reader does not have. title: Example Use Cases
text:
Product questions from website visitors. A prospective customer arrives on the website and asks whether the platform can separate public and internal knowledge. The chatbot retrieves the relevant passages, answers directly, and offers to route the visitor to a human if their question goes beyond published material.

Policy retrieval. An employee asks what the internal policy says about a particular situation. The chatbot retrieves the passage from the internal scope — available to them because they are authenticated and public visitors are not — and answers with the relevant clause rather than a link to a forty-page document.

Employee workflow automation. An employee asks the chatbot to complete a routine process: raising a request, notifying the responsible team, and confirming that it has been done. The agent decomposes the task, calls the tools required in sequence, confirms the consequential step with the user, and reports what was completed.

Multi-step question answering. A user asks a question whose answer requires two or three facts that live in different documents. A single retrieval would answer half of it. The agent retrieves, notices the gap, searches again for the missing part, and composes a complete answer from both sets of passages.

Notification routing. A website visitor describes a need that the published material does not cover. Rather than ending the conversation, the chatbot collects the necessary detail, sends an email to the appropriate internal recipient, and tells the visitor who will follow up and roughly when.

title: Frequently Asked Questions, in Prose
questions: How does it know the answers?
text:
What does the chatbot do? It answers questions, retrieves company knowledge, navigates websites, and performs actions such as sending emails, notifying teams, and executing workflows on behalf of customers, employees, partners, and stakeholders.

How does it know the answers? It retrieves relevant company documents using Retrieval-Augmented Generation before generating a response. The customer's material is indexed in advance; at question time the most relevant passages are found and supplied to the language model, which answers from them. It is not relying on general knowledge absorbed during training.

Can it perform actions? Yes. Beyond answering, it can send emails, notify teams, and execute workflows. Which actions are available in any given deployment is determined by the tools the customer has enabled and the permissions of the person asking, and consequential actions are configured to require confirmation.

Who can use it? Customers, employees, stakeholders, and partners, depending on configured permissions. The same deployment can serve several of these audiences with different knowledge scopes and different available actions.

What makes it different from FAQ bots? It performs semantic retrieval, reasoning, and task execution instead of keyword matching. A FAQ bot returns a stored answer when it recognises a stored question; this platform finds meaning-relevant passages in real documents, reasons across them, and can change the state of the world by carrying out a task.

Is it GDPR compliant? The platform is built around GDPR principles — transparency, lawful processing, purpose limitation, data minimisation, user rights, and configurable access controls — and the company acts as data processor under a data processing agreement in customer deployments. Compliance in any specific deployment also depends on how the customer, as controller, configures and uses it. Details are in Section 18.

title: Glossary
text:
Agent. A language model given a goal, a set of tools, and the ability to choose which tools to use in which order, observing each result before deciding the next step.

Agentic AI. An AI system that plans and executes multi-step tasks rather than only producing a single response to a single prompt.

Chunk. A passage of text, produced by dividing a source document, that forms the unit of storage and retrieval in a RAG system.

Embedding. A numerical vector representing the meaning of a piece of text, such that texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together.

Grounding. The practice of requiring a model to base its answer on supplied source material rather than on its own parametric memory.

Hallucination. Fluent output from a language model that is not supported by the supplied context or by fact.

Hybrid search. Retrieval that combines semantic vector similarity with keyword matching, in order to handle both paraphrase and exact identifiers well.

Knowledge scope. A labelled subset of the indexed corpus, used to control which users may retrieve which content.

Large Language Model (LLM). A model trained on large volumes of text that generates language and performs reasoning over text supplied to it.

Prompt injection. An attack in which text within user input or retrieved content attempts to override the system's instructions.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). An architecture in which relevant documents are retrieved at question time and supplied to a language model as context before it generates an answer.

Semantic search. Search that matches meaning rather than exact wording, performed by comparing embeddings.

Tool calling. The mechanism by which a language model requests that a defined function be executed, with the platform validating and performing the execution.

Vector database. A store that holds embeddings and finds nearest neighbours in high-dimensional space efficiently.

Workflow automation. The execution of a defined multi-step business process, potentially spanning several systems, triggered from within a conversation.
